nameStory: The 'speckled greenshield' name perfectly captures this lichen's appearance - it forms greenish, shield-like patches decorated with tiny white speckles across its surface. These speckles are actually special breathing pores called pseudocyphellae that help the lichen exchange gases with the air. The shield part of the name refers to how it grows flat against tree bark like a protective shield.
description: Speckled Greenshield is a leafy lichen that grows flat against tree bark in circular or irregular patches. It has a greenish-gray color with distinctive tiny white dots scattered across its surface like someone sprinkled salt on it. The lichen forms lobed, leaf-like structures that can spread several inches across, creating an attractive mosaic pattern on tree trunks. It belongs to a large family of shield lichens that are common throughout New England's forests.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for tiny white speckles (pseudocyphellae) scattered across the greenish surface - they feel slightly rough to the touch and look like pinpricks of white paint

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms flat, leafy lobes that lie closely against the bark with slightly raised, wavy edges that you can gently lift with your fingernail

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Greenish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found on the bark of deciduous trees, especially oaks and maples, rarely on rocks or conifers

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches can grow 2-6 inches across, often merging with neighboring patches to cover large sections of trunk

habitat: Look for Speckled Greenshield on the bark of mature hardwood trees in New England's mixed and deciduous forests, particularly on oaks, maples, and other broad-leaved trees. It prefers trees in somewhat open areas with good air circulation rather than dense, humid forest interiors. You'll often find it on the main trunks and larger branches of trees in parks, forest edges, and suburban woodlands.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant green as spring rains moisten it. This is an excellent time to see the color contrast between the green body and white speckles.
seasonality.summer: Often appears grayish and duller during dry periods, but the white speckles remain clearly visible. Look for it during humid mornings when dew brings out the green tones.
seasonality.fall: Still easily spotted as leaves fall away, revealing lichen-covered tree trunks. The white speckles stand out well against autumn's brown backdrop.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round on bare tree trunks. Snow and ice can temporarily obscure it, but it's often one of the most noticeable colorful things on winter trees.

funFact: The tiny white speckles that give this lichen its name are actually sophisticated air vents that can open and close like microscopic windows, allowing the lichen to control its gas exchange and water balance - essentially, it's breathing through hundreds of tiny pores!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other shield lichens that lack the distinctive white speckles. Remember: if you don't see those tiny white dots scattered across the surface, it's probably a different species. The speckles are like this lichen's fingerprint - no other common New England lichen has quite the same pattern.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name reveals this lichen's taxonomic journey - it was shuffled between different genera as scientists better understood lichen relationships, finally landing in its own genus Flavopunctelia in the 1980s. This reflects how lichen classification is still actively evolving as we learn more about these complex organisms.
compareHints: Speckled Greenshield differs from its close relative, Powder-edged Speckled Greenshield, by lacking the powdery soredia (reproductive dust) along the lobe edges that the latter species displays. While both have the characteristic white speckles, Powder-edged Speckled Greenshield looks like someone dusted its edges with flour. If you see white powder at the margins, you've found the other species.
